format: Six-player, one-GM. Each player runs two characters: a school-age kid and a multi-storey combat mech.
elevatorPitch: Six players, one GM, Starfinder Second Edition. Each player runs two characters: a kid (starts at level 1, seventeen years old, legally draft-eligible for the city's civil defense corps) and a Frame — a multi-storey combat mech, fixed at level 12, built as a full PC with its own class. The kids' school lives, relationships, and personal choices directly gate how much of their Frame's power they can actually use in a fight. Same emotional shape as Neon Genesis Evangelion, run through Starfinder's bounded-accuracy math instead of anime logic — "legally distinct" setting and mechanics throughout.

systemNotes.context: Starfinder Second Edition has no official mech rules — this system is bespoke. (Starfinder Tech Core, the next major rulebook, adds starship combat and tech classes but not mechs.) The game inherits Pathfinder 2e's math: attack bonus, AC, DCs, and HP scale tightly and predictably with level, and the four degrees of success amplify small numeric gaps into large narrative ones. A level gap much past 4-5 becomes "cannot participate," not "outmatched."
designPrinciples: A level-1 kid cannot be given a numeric bonus that meaningfully affects a level-12 fight, and shouldn't be — that breaks bounded accuracy.

A level-12 Frame cannot be treated as gear worn by a level-1 kid — item bonuses stack on the wielder's own proficiency, so a Frame-as-equipment would still swing like a level-1 character. The Frame has to be its own character.
The gap between kid and Frame is a feature, not something to balance away. The system's job is to make both halves matter without ever letting them touch the same math.

kid.advancement: Advances by narrative milestone (roughly one level per major arc/Contact event), not XP budget.
kid.legalFraming: Seventeen is the age the city's charter allows conscription into civil defense roles. The kids are here legally. Nobody is breaking a rule to put them in a cockpit — that's the horror register: procedural, not criminal.

frame.buildMethod: Built as a full PC using a standard SF2e class — not a monster stat block, not upscaled gear. Pick a class, build it exactly as any PC of the same level, then reflavor: a Strike is a building-sized fist, a spell is a kilometre-wide effect.
frame.advancement: Fixed at level 12 only through the six-day opening arc (data/episodes) — there isn't time for a full defeat-and-refit cycle in six days. From Day 7 onward, Frames level up in lockstep with their pilot's own milestone leveling across the campaign's 8-level arc (see design/campaign-arc.md), gated by a significant Claimant defeat plus enough downtime to refit. Independently of level, a Frame also only unlocks access to abilities it already statistically has as its pilot's Resonance rises — a level-12 (or higher) Frame at 30% Resonance is still only allowed to use a fraction of its sheet.
frame.classAssignment: Open question — see open-questions.json (frame-class-assignment): player-chosen, or assigned by the Directorate's psychological profiling as a verdict on the kid.

campaignStructure.openingArc: Days 1-6 are hand-placed (see /data/episodes) and do not use the Contact Pool roll.
campaignStructure.postOpeningArc: From Day 7 onward, the hand-placed opening arc ends and the Contact Pool (see campaign/config.json) takes over as the procedural engine driving the rest of the campaign.
